doc.title: Hinton Milt — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Louis Armstrong, Basie and New York studio scene
title: The Metropole bandstand, soul food across the street and the contacts it brought
summary: Taylor and Hinton recall the bar-top bandstand at the Metropole, where contractors found Hinton for record dates.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah, he was something else. One of the great eating places we‟re talking about right across the street from the Metropoll was a place called the Copperwayo.

There was a lady… there was so many brothers working in the Metropoll, this lady was cooking soul food. She had the best collard greens in town. You could step right out of the Metropoll and go across the street. Della was her name at the Copperwayo and eat you some good soul food dinner.
That was, the Metropoll was a strange place to play because everybody was across the scene. I mean you were spread out. There was no…you were all right over the bar.

And going up against the wall over there. And people standing down at the bar, you were blowing over the heads and people sitting at the tables are back there. But people came in there didn‟t just see the jazz, they would see the kind of musician. I mean Jean Cooper played there.
The whole Woody Herman‟s band played there.

We would line up along that bar like it was a prisoner‟s… and played. It was quite interesting. But I will tell you the contact was wonderful. I got a lot of gigs, a lot of record dates out of that. Contractors would come by there and…

They would say, “That‟s Milt over there.” The guy would come in and have a beer and wait until the break and would say, “What are you doing tomorrow?” He would make a record date. One day I saw Lou [unintelligible] and [unintelligible] sitting in there having a beer.
In the Metropoll. They were sitting right by the door. I couldn‟t believe it. He couldn‟t hardly speak English.
